experiment.hypothesis: the append path's atomic rename makes concurrent appends safe
experiment.setup: mktemp scratch directories via --dir, concurrent-append trials against workflow-state.php
experiment.assumptions: no lock/lease/CAS exists (documented in the header)
experiment.method: technical Architecture review reproduced the race
experiment.result: 23/30 trials silently lost a transition; the losing process still exited 0 reporting success; every surviving sequence stayed dense and monotonic
experiment.interpretation: a dense, monotonic sequence number does not prove no record was lost, because the clobbering writer reuses the lost writer's sequence number
experiment.limitations: reproduced only in scratch directories, not against the production corpus
experiment.conclusion: the absolute completeness claim is withdrawn; only 'no record lost relative to the frozen manifest and observed inputs' is provable

anchor: first measured CPU-only prototype benchmark: English-approval, German-approval, English-rejection, German-rejection sentences parsed at roughly 0.001-0.0015 ms mean latency each.
statement: The first genuinely measured (not estimated) data point in the semantic-compiler research thread, explicitly caveated as measuring rule-engine overhead for a tiny grammar, not a production semantic compiler.

experiment.hypothesis: a deterministic semantic-compiler prototype can parse simple sentences at very low latency on CPU
experiment.setup: a small deterministic rule-based parser with a handful of rules for approval/rejection sentences in English and German
experiment.assumptions: the grammar covers only the tested sentence patterns
experiment.inputs: 4 test sentences (English approval, German approval, English rejection, German rejection)
experiment.method: measured wall-clock parse latency on the execution environment
experiment.result: ~1-2 microseconds per sentence; the German rule failed to extract the causal condition that the English rule caught (condition:null vs condition:audit_no_critical_vulnerabilities)
experiment.interpretation: the computational model is cheap; the semantic model (cross-lingual grammar coverage) is hard
experiment.limitations: tiny grammar with only a handful of rules; not representative of a complete semantic compiler
experiment.conclusion: speed is not the bottleneck; semantic/grammar coverage is

anchor: KOS-SCB v0.1 proposed test categories: word-order variation, English<->German, active<->passive, meaning-changing sentences, context (temporal/causal/concessive), and contradiction.

anchor: the LLM does not get to directly write KnowledgeOS knowledge. It proposes a semantic interpretation. The compiler validates it.

anchor: KOS-SCB v0.1 measured result: 120 test cases, 74.2% overall semantic accuracy, mean parsing latency 0.0081 ms (median 0.0057 ms, P95 0.0093 ms), ~123,000 parses/sec, peak traced Python memory ~0.05 MB; 6 false accepts among 20 deliberately ambiguous cases.
statement: The first full measured KOS-SCB benchmark run, broken down by capability (expression equivalence 70%, meaning changes 80%, context preservation 75%, safe abstention 70%); interpreted as demonstrating that the computational model is cheap while the semantic model is hard.

experiment.hypothesis: a single-layer text-to-KIR pattern-matching compiler can achieve useful semantic accuracy
experiment.setup: KOS-SCB v0.1, a deterministic pattern-matching parser mapping text directly to KIR
experiment.inputs: 120 controlled test cases across expression-equivalence, meaning-change, context-preservation, and ambiguous/abstention categories
experiment.method: measured accuracy per category plus latency/throughput/memory on CPU
experiment.result: 74.2% overall accuracy, ~123k parses/sec, 6/20 false accepts on ambiguous cases
experiment.interpretation: the architecture is extremely fast but the semantic grammar is incomplete; jumping directly from text to KIR skips intermediate representations needed for accuracy
experiment.limitations: primitive single-layer grammar, no type system, no context binding, no epistemic validation, no UNKNOWN state
experiment.conclusion: the next version must add Surface AST -> Semantic AST -> Type System -> Context Binding -> Epistemic Validation stages rather than optimize the single layer further

anchor: accuracy improvements from adding layers are not additive: 74.2% + 20% + 10% + 25% + 15% + 19% + 25% -> ~95% is not a valid statistical inference, because later stages can fix the same failures earlier stages already fixed (overlapping gains).
statement: A reviewer's explicit rejection of an intermediate turn's own additive-accuracy-projection table, reclassifying the claimed 93-95% figure from 'projected accuracy' to 'target hypothesis requiring measurement'.

anchor: semantic accuracy != epistemic correctness: the compiler can correctly interpret 'the architect approved the design' (semantic interpretation = correct) while KnowledgeOS must still return epistemic status = UNKNOWN because there is no evidence.
statement: A fundamental distinction the benchmark surfaced: understanding an expression correctly is not the same question as whether there are sufficient grounds to believe the claim it expresses.

anchor: the biggest discovery: UNKNOWN is more important than accuracy -- a false-acceptance rate near 30% (system says 'I understand' when it only pattern-matched) is more dangerous than a lower raw accuracy score.
statement: Connects the benchmark's false-accept problem directly to the Zero principle made operational: a system saying UNKNOWN is more intelligent than one producing a wrong certainty.

anchor: the KnowledgeOS Kernel should remain the domain/constitutional core; Epistemic Validation machinery is an enforcement mechanism operating at that boundary, not itself 'the kernel' -- 'KOS-EV' should not be named 'the KnowledgeOS kernel' yet.
statement: A DDD-altitude-discipline correction of an intermediate proposal that had prematurely labeled the epistemic-validation stage as the kernel.

anchor: KOS-SCB v0.2 toy-simulation result: 1,000 synthetic cases, overall invariance score 80.0%, expression equivalence 66.7%, semantic distinction 100%, context preservation 100%, transformation preservation 100%, temporal distinction 100%, unknown/ambiguity handling 100%, contradiction handling 0%, abst

experiment.hypothesis: a semantic compiler can be measured on invariance, non-collapse, transformation-preservation, and contradiction handling as separate dimensions rather than one 'accuracy' number
experiment.setup: synthetic 1,000-case corpus across ten semantic families with equivalence/distinction/context/transformation/temporal/ambiguity/contradiction variants
experiment.assumptions: contradiction handling can be tested at the compiler layer
experiment.method: toy deterministic parser scored per dimension
experiment.result: non-collapse succeeded (100% on semantic distinction) but contradiction handling scored 0%; expression-equivalence convergence only 66.7%
experiment.interpretation: contradiction detection is not primarily a compiler-layer responsibility (requires same-subject + compatible-scope + incompatible-proposition test, which belongs to the KnowledgeOS epistemic layer); equivalence convergence needs a real semantic-role grammar, not pattern matching
experiment.limitations: toy/synthetic, not a production NLP system; throughput number has no architectural significance
experiment.conclusion: remove 'contradiction detection' from the Semantic Compiler benchmark as a primary compiler responsibility; redefine success criteria as five properties (semantic invariance, semantic non-collapse, epistemic non-invention, identity preservation, contradiction integrity) rather than one accuracy percentage

statement: Replaces the earlier 'target 95% accuracy' success criterion with five distinct, separately-measured properties, explicitly rejecting a single composite score.

anchor: keep the Semantic Compiler outside the constitutional kernel: the compiler can be replaced; the kernel cannot -- this protects KnowledgeOS from becoming 'a sophisticated NLP system with philosophical decoration.'
statement: A firm boundary rule for the Semantic Compiler's placement relative to the constitutional core, with an explicit feedback loop (architecture hypothesis -> prototype -> observed failure -> KEEP/MOVE/REJECT classification) for using experimental evidence without letting it redesign the kernel prematurely.

anchor: six-way separation: identity != role != eligibility != authorization != ownership != continuation.
statement: The design principle of the AST-017 session-bootstrap resolver: six distinct concepts kept as separate first-class report blocks so that none silently substitutes for another (e.g. identity never reaches a gate as a grant).

statement: States the resolver's core structural guarantee later independently falsification-tested in S0315: a single narrowly-bounded exception to full delegation, and no dependency on which LLM provider is running the session.

anchor: the divergence is NOT model-dependent. Two AI providers working the same repository, same workflow records, same injected context resolve the same governed session differently -- and both cannot. The defect is coordination legibility, not model capability.
statement: The measured finding motivating the entire session-bootstrap correction saga: session-resolve.php returned AMBIGUOUS with 4 candidates for a session that genuinely held its lane, because process identity lived only in free-text executionContext with no queryable handoff-fact.

anchor: the recorded refusals ('I will not adopt another process's identity in order to become operable') were correct under the rules. The tooling gave those sessions no lawful way to proceed.

anchor: poison-test methodology: inject decoy fields (fake mutationOwner, workItemState, sessions dict, top-level authorizationLinkage, a decoy 'handoffs' array outside transitions) into a valid workflow record and verify the resolver reports only from the documented derived fields, ignoring every decoy.
statement: A falsification methodology (labelled F1-F14 plus L1-L3 live-record probes) for verifying that a resolver reads exactly its documented inputs and no more; found the resolver's handoff read is a strict subset of the underlying fold's handoffsTo, so it can only ever over-report 'not ready', never under-report.

anchor: three distinct uncertainties must not be conflated: model/interpretation uncertainty ('which interpretation should I choose'), representational uncertainty ('does my representation capture the meaning'), and epistemic uncertainty ('is this justified') -- the semantic compiler should expose the first
statement: Refines the Bayesian semantic-entropy proposal by noting that low entropy over a compiler's own candidate-interpretation space does not mean the expression is objectively unambiguous -- it only means the model's own candidate set has low uncertainty.

anchor: false convergence (semantic collision) is more dangerous than false divergence: if two equivalent sentences produce different SNFs, that is inefficiency; if two different propositions produce the same SNF, that is knowledge corruption.
statement: A stated safety asymmetry motivating the introduction of a hard non-collapse safety gate (rather than a weighted composite score that could average away a catastrophic collapse) and a proposed 'Semantic Collision Rate' metric.

anchor: do NOT use a weighted harmonic-mean composite SNF score; instead impose a hard safety constraint (non-collapse below threshold => FAIL, independent of the other metrics) plus descriptive metrics for the surviving system.
statement: Rejects the mathematically-elegant but architecturally-dangerous idea of averaging convergence/non-collapse/transformation/entropy into one quality score, on the grounds that a catastrophic non-collapse failure must never be diluted by good scores elsewhere.

anchor: 100-case synthetic pilot result: semantic collision rate 25% (5 of 20 deliberately distinct-meaning pairs collapsed to the same synthetic SNF); 0/20 distinct-meaning pairs passed the non-collapse threshold.
statement: A deliberately-seeded synthetic pilot demonstrating that the measurement framework mechanically detects injected semantic collisions; explicitly caveated as testing the measurement mathematics only, not whether SNF actually preserves semantics (which requires a real semantic distance, not a synthetic structural one).

experiment.hypothesis: the proposed multi-metric measurement framework mechanically detects seeded semantic collisions
experiment.setup: 100 synthetic cases (20 true equivalences, 20 deliberate semantic collisions, 15 word-order transformations, 15 context changes, 10 ambiguities, 10 contradictions, 10 unknown/unrepresentable) with a synthetic structural distance function
experiment.assumptions: synthetic SNF representations and distances stand in for a real semantic distance
experiment.method: computed C_snf/NC_snf/CR/T_snf/H_sem on the synthetic corpus
experiment.result: semantic collision rate 25% (5/20 deliberately-collapsed pairs detected); 0/20 non-collapse threshold passes
experiment.interpretation: a composite quality score would hide this failure (e.g. C=0.99,T=0.98,H=0.05 but NC=0 looks excellent yet is a collision) -- non-collapse must be a hard gate
experiment.limitations: the SNF representations and distances are synthetic, not derived from a real semantic parser
experiment.conclusion: the measurement framework works mechanically; whether SNF actually preserves semantics remains untested and requires a gold-relation/confusion-matrix experiment (proposed as v0.3) rather than immediately scaling to 1,000 real cases

anchor: gold-relation / confusion-matrix design (v0.3): compare SNF's EQUIVALENT/DISTINCT/UNKNOWN judgment against an independently-labelled gold relation, producing three failure classes -- false divergence, semantic collision, and false certainty (UNKNOWN converted into confident interpretation).
statement: A proposed next experiment testing whether SNF agrees with independently-established ground truth about semantic relations, rather than only self-consistency of the SNF metric.
